balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Baker Hughes Company: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Baker Hughes Company: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Baker Hughes Company: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Baker Hughes Company: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Baker Hughes Company: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Baker Hughes Company: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Baker Hughes Company: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Baker Hughes Company: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue
segmentRevenue.content:
Revenue split across Baker Hughes's three reporting segments: OFSE (Oilfield Services & Equipment -- drilling, completions, production, subsea), IET (Industrial & Energy Technology -- gas technology/turbomachinery, climate/new energy), and Chart (Chart Industries, consolidated mid-July 2026).

For Baker Hughes: OFSE is roughly 48% of revenue and the more oil-price-cyclical piece; IET is roughly 40% with large multi-year order books; Chart only has data from Q3 2026 onward and contributed about 11% of revenue (~$888m) in its first full quarter, split roughly 70% original equipment / 30% aftermarket.

What to watch:

  • Chart's revenue run-rate as integration proceeds versus the ~$325m annualised cost-synergy target
  • Mix shift toward IET/Chart's longer-cycle, less oil-price-sensitive revenue versus OFSE

segmentEbitda.title: Segment EBITDA
segmentEbitda.content:
EBITDA by segment -- the profitability each of OFSE, IET and Chart is generating before the corporate-level roll-up.

For Baker Hughes: management guides Chart segment EBITDA margin toward 22-23% by H2 2028 as integration and cost synergies land; comparing Chart's margin against OFSE/IET each quarter is the near-term read on whether that deal is tracking.

What to watch:

  • Chart margin trajectory toward the 22-23% H2 2028 target
  • OFSE margin resilience through the oil-price cycle versus IET's steadier margin on backlog-covered revenue

segmentOrders.title: Orders by segment
segmentOrders.content:
New orders booked in the period by segment -- the leading indicator for future segment revenue, since IET and Chart revenue is substantially backlog-driven.

For Baker Hughes: the Gas Tech Equipment line is a sub-component already included inside IET orders (it is shown for colour on the turbomachinery cycle, not as a fourth segment to sum).

What to watch:

  • IET order lumpiness -- single large LNG/turbomachinery awards can swing a quarter
  • Chart order intake once it has a full year of comparable quarters
  • Book-to-bill (orders vs revenue) by segment

segmentRpo.title: Remaining performance obligations (RPO / backlog)
segmentRpo.content:
RPO is contracted revenue not yet recognised -- the backlog that converts to future segment revenue. Shown in total and split by segment.

For Baker Hughes: IET carries the bulk of RPO ($39.4bn at Q3 2026, a record) reflecting multi-year LNG and turbomachinery contracts; OFSE's RPO is much smaller and shorter-cycle; Chart's backlog only appears from Q3 2026.

What to watch:

  • IET RPO growth versus IET revenue -- a widening gap signals future revenue visibility
  • Chart RPO once two or more quarters are comparable

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Baker Hughes Company: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Baker Hughes Company: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
